items.bodyEn: West of Goyu the road runs under the Goyu pine colonnade, planted on shogunate orders in 1604 to shade travelers; about 600 meters survive, a National Natural Monument since 1944. At its end lies Akasaka, only about 1.7 kilometers away — the shortest gap between two Tōkaidō stations, which made the towns fierce rivals for guests.
items.sourceNote: Goyu pine colonnade, National Natural Monument, 1944; Edo-period Tōkaidō dōchūki

items.bodyEn: Hiroshige's Goyu print, 'Travelers Stopped by Women', shows two inn touts hauling reluctant men off the street by sleeve and belt while earlier arrivals settle in behind them. With Akasaka a short walk away, Goyu's inns lived or died by such hustling. Hiroshige hid a joke on the inn's signboard: it advertises his print series and its publisher.

旅籠 (hatago) meant the basket (籠) that carried a horse's fodder on a journey (旅). It shifted to the traveler's own packed food, then to the meal an inn served, and at last to the inn itself, the 旅籠屋. A hatago included supper and breakfast; at the cheaper 木賃宿 you paid only for firewood (木賃) and cooked your rice.
items.sourceNote: Kōjien / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten, entries はたご (旅籠) and きちんやど (木賃宿)

items.bodyEn: Japanese sorts its mimetic words in two: 擬音語 (giongo) copy sounds — ざあざあ for rain, わんわん for a dog, ゴロゴロ for thunder — while 擬態語 (gitaigo) picture states, like にこにこ for a smile. Sound words lean toward katakana, state words toward hiragana, a habit rather than a rule. Most take と before a verb or する after: ざあざあと降る, どきどきする.
items.ja: {雨|あめ}がざあざあ{降|ふ}っている。
items.kana: あめがざあざあふっている。
